measures.questionText:
The Bothell City Council adopted Resolution No. 1784, approving annexation into the Shoreline Fire Department Regional Fire Authority and related plan amendment. To maintain current fire and emergency medical service levels and provide long-term financial and operational sustainability for such services within Bothell, should Bothell be annexed into and become a part of the Shoreline Fire Department Regional Fire Authority, effective March 1, 2027, pursuant to the plan amendment, as provided in Resolution No. 1784?
Yes No
measures.officialStatement: The Bothell City Council adopted Resolution 1784 requesting voter approval to annex into and become part of the Shoreline Fire Department Regional Fire Authority ("RFA"). As the region has grown and costs have increased, Bothell has considered governance/service models for fire and emergency medical services (“EMS”). As part of its study, Bothell contracted with the RFA for fire administration (Fire Chief) services. The City Council has determined that annexing into the RFA ensures long-term sustainability of funding to maintain current fire protection and EMS service levels. Annexation will not change the delivery or the level of services to Bothell residents. If annexation is approved, Bothell Fire Department would become part of the larger RFA, instead of operating as a standalone, smaller fire department. By combining resources and expertise and coordinating efforts, fire and EMS service can gain efficiencies, including response operations. Bothell voters will be entitled to vote on all ballot measures proposed by the RFA—including those pertaining to taxation and benefit charges. Bothell will have representation on the RFA Board. If annexation is rejected, Bothell would need to reseek voter approval, negotiate a new agreement with RFA or another agency, or reconstitute the Bothell Fire Department. https://bothellwa.gov/2209/Fire-Service-Study

To fund public safety and land use services, and to remain an independent city, the Clyde Hill City Council passed Resolution No. 725 proposing an increase to its regular property tax levy from approximately $0.30 to $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed valuation for 2027 with 3% annual increases to the annual limit factor for 2028-2036. Exemptions apply to seniors, veterans, and disabled persons who qualify under RCW 84.36.381. Should this proposition be approved?
Yes No
measures.officialStatement: Clyde Hill Resolution No. 725 asks voters to increase the City’s portion of property taxes to pay for police, fire, emergency medical services, 911 dispatch, land use, and zoning services. Clyde Hill has the third lowest levy rate in King County, receiving less than $0.05 of every $1.00 paid in property taxes. A resident-led Financial Sustainability Task Force concluded that the City cut expenses where it could and kept staffing lean compared to similar sized cities. It concluded that further reductions threaten basic services and legal requirements. Without additional revenues, Clyde Hill will not have the requisite funds to remain an independent city with local control of its police department and zoning issues, as well as the quality fire and emergency medical services residents have come to expect. If approved, Clyde Hill’s property tax levy rate would increase from $0.29548 per $1,000 of assessed valuation in 2026 to a levy rate not to exceed $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed valuation in 2027. This equates to about a $225 increase in the city’s portion of property taxes per $1,000,000 of assessed valuation. In 2028-2036, the total regular property levy amount would increase by a limit factor of 3% annually. The final levy in 2036 will become the base for establishing levy rates for following years. If this proposition is rejected, the City is projected to run out of operating funds by the end of 2030. It will be unable to sustain current service levels and may need to consider dissolution.

measures.officialStatement: The City of Issaquah is proposing to issue up to $18 million of bonds for various park, trail, and recreation projects. If approved by voters, these park bonds would replace the City’s retiring park bonds and mature 20 years after they are issued. The proposed park bond projects include: sports fields and courts at a variety of locations; new trails on Cougar and Squak mountains that connect to surrounding regional trails, trailhead improvements for West Tiger Mountain; restoration of Confluence Park’s Ek House; playground improvements and a new dog park at Tibbetts Valley Park; and related capital improvements. All of these projects were identified as community priorities in the adopted 2024 Park System Plan. The City proposes issuing the new bonds as the prior bonds mature to keep property taxes similar, meaning the estimated cost to a $1 million homeowner would average about $80 per year. Low-income seniors, certain veterans and others who qualify for tax exemptions from the retiring bonds would continue to be exempt. For more information, go to issaquahwa.gov/parkbond.

Kenmore City Council passed Ordinance 26-0644 regarding funding for programing and services. To fund Climate & Environmental Stewardship, Affordable Housing, and Human Services, this proposition increases Kenmore’s maximum regular property tax levy rate to $1.25/$1,000 for collection in 2027; sets the limit factor for Kenmore’s regular property tax levy increases in 2028-2032 to 6%; authorizes the 2032 levy amount as the basis to calculate subsequent levies (RCW 84.55); and exempts qualifying seniors, veterans, and others (RCW 84.36). Should this proposition be approved?
Yes No
measures.officialStatement: The City of Kenmore seeks voter approval to increase the City’s regular property tax levy up to $1.25 per $1,000 of assessed value to fund programs and services for Climate & Environmental Stewardship, Affordable Housing, and Human Services. Under state law, without voter approval, a city may increase its regular property tax levy amount by only 1% each year, which has not kept pace with inflation and costs of providing City programs and services. If approved, Proposition 1 would authorize the increase of the City’s levy rate by approximately $0.36 per $1,000 assessed value, for a total regular property tax rate not to exceed $1.25 per $1,000 assessed value for collection in 2027, and allow the levy amount to increase by up to 6% in the succeeding five years (2028-2032). The total rate may not exceed the maximum property tax levy rate allowed to cities by state law. The 2032 levy amount would be the basis to calculate subsequent levies. The increase in the City’s regular property tax levy, combined with cost-cutting measures by the City, will promote financial sustainability for City operations and programs. Proposition 1 would add approximately $30 per month to the property tax bill for a home assessed at Kenmore’s average value of $1,000,000. Proposition 1 would exempt qualifying seniors, veterans, and others from the increase.

The City Council of the City of Lake Forest Park adopted Resolution No. 26-2084 to fund Public Safety Services. This proposition would fund Public Safety Services per the Resolution including police services, safety equipment, 911 dispatch, emergency management services, jail services, and mental health crisis response by temporarily setting the maximum total regular levy rate at $0.88920/$1,000 for collection in 2027, with annual increases for five years based on inflation (Seattle region CPI-U). Qualifying low-income seniors, disabled veterans, and other disabled persons are exempt under RCW 84.36.381. Should this proposition be approved?
Yes No
measures.officialStatement: The City of Lake Forest Park proposes Proposition 1 to provide sustainable funding for Public Safety Services including: police staffing, training, and safety equipment; 911 dispatch services; jail services; prosecution and public defense costs; and crisis intervention and mental health response programs. Proposition 1 would temporarily authorize an annual increase of approximately $1.2 million in the City’s regular property tax levy through a levy lid lift. Without a voter approved levy lid lift, the City is limited to increasing its tax levy by 1%. The additional levy funds from Proposition 1 would be tracked separately and could only be used to pay for the cost of Public Safety Services. Proposition 1 would cost property owners $0.22 per $1,000 of assessed valuation ($22 per $100,000). In 2027, for a $963,000 median value home this would be about $211.86 annually or $17.66 per month. For each of the next five years (2028 – 2032), the levy lid lift could be increased by the rate of inflation, which requires an open public process and a council vote to approve. Proposition 1 exempts qualifying seniors, disabled veterans and others with disabilities from the levy increase. When Proposition 1 expires, the levy will decrease to what it would have been if never approved and the City had only taken the 1% increase authorized by state law.

The City Council of the City of SeaTac passed Ordinance No. 26-1017 concerning funding for public safety and other City services. If approved, this proposition would increase the City’s sales and use tax rate by 1/10th of 1% (0.1%) to provide funding for public safety services, including but not limited to, fire protection, fire prevention and emergency medical response; law enforcement support and staffing and retention; criminal justice purposes; public safety operations, maintenance and capital; and other public safety operations and services authorized under RCW 82.14.450. Should this proposition be approved?
Yes No
measures.officialStatement: The City of SeaTac provides public safety and related services directly and through contracts with the Puget Sound Regional Fire Authority and King County Sheriff’s Office. These services support residents and thousands of people who travel to SeaTac daily to access local hotels, restaurants, businesses, employment opportunities, and the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, located entirely within the City. This influx produces a daily visitor population more than six times the City’s residential population. Serving residents and travelers results in a disproportionately high number of complex fire and emergency medical incidents and increases demands on public safety services. Inflation and hazardous workplace conditions have increased the cost of these services. City revenues have not kept pace, and additional resources are needed to continue providing critical fire, medical and public safety services. Proposition 1 would authorize a 0.1% sales and use tax on taxable retail sales and uses within SeaTac. The tax would apply to taxable purchases by residents and travelers. Only transactions taxable under Washington law would be taxed; most groceries are exempt. State law also exempts motor vehicle sales and the first 36 months of vehicle leases from this tax. Revenue from the tax would be shared 85% to the City and 15% to King County. At least one-third of the revenue would be used solely for fire protection purposes, criminal justice purposes, or both, as required by RCW 82.14.450. This tax would add $0.10 to a taxable $100 purchase.

This proposition would create the Shoreline Metropolitan Park District to finance and refinance the acquisition, construction, operation, maintenance, programming, renovation, and expansion of a pool facility and future recreational facilities. The District, with the same boundaries as Shoreline, governed by a Board composed of City Councilmembers, would exercise powers in state law, provide ongoing funding, levy regular property taxes not to exceed $0.75/$1,000 assessed valuation (anticipated initial rate $0.55/$1,000, or as necessary to generate approximately $8.8 million annually). Should the Shoreline Metropolitan Park District be formed?
For the formation of a Shoreline Metropolitan Park District to be governed by Shoreline City Councilmembers. Against the formation of a Shoreline Metropolitan Park District.
measures.officialStatement: If approved by voters, this proposition creates the Shoreline Metropolitan Park District (MPD) to finance and refinance the construction, operation, and maintenance of a new indoor pool facility and potential future recreational facilities. The MPD would have the same boundaries as the City of Shoreline (City). The MPD would be a new taxing jurisdiction (RCW 35.61) governed by a board composed of City Councilmembers. City staff would operate and maintain the pool pursuant to an agreement with the MPD. The approximately 48,000 square foot facility would be built on City-owned property at 17828 Midvale Ave N. The preliminary accessible design includes an 8-lane lap pool with diving well; recreation pool with a lazy river for walking and floating; warmer hydrotherapy pool; sauna; universal changerooms; party rooms; parking; and outdoor spaces connecting to the Interurban Trail. Creating the MPD would allow for construction of future recreational facilities should additional funding be available. The pool facility design leaves space for a potential recreation facility addition. The anticipated initial property tax levy rate is $0.55/$1,000 assessed valuation, or as necessary to generate approximately $8.8 million annually. The maximum allowable rate is $0.75/$1,000. Revenue would pay for pool facility construction, operation, and maintenance. Revenue could only be used for the pool facility and future recreational facilities, not other City needs. Tax collection would start in 2028. A homeowner with a median value home ($831,000 in 2026) would pay approximately $421 per year, an average of $35 per month, in additional property taxes.

measures.officialStatement: Proposition 1 authorizes school construction bonds to replace and rebuild deteriorating schools and make districtwide safety and accessibility improvements and upgrades. Proposition 1 will improve student, staff and community safety, security and accessibility, enhance student learning environments, improve and expand educational opportunities, and provide necessary student educational facilities (including career/technical learning spaces). The bonds will allow Highline Public Schools to: (1) address critical needs districtwide, including core building system upgrades and site improvements (plumbing, hot water systems, HVAC, electrical, roofing, security, fire systems and earthquake safety upgrades); (2) construct a new school to replace Sylvester Middle School; (3) construct a new school to replace Cascade Middle School; (4) partially rebuild and modernize Chinook Middle School (replacing the oldest, most outdated buildings, facilities and infrastructure with new construction; renovating and updating existing usable buildings; and replacing portables with permanent classrooms); (5) rebuild and modernize the former Southern Heights Elementary School site as a new facility for CHOICE Academy; and (6) develop design plans for construction, redevelopment or replacement of Valley View Early Learning Center and Hilltop Elementary School. More information is available at highlineschools.org/bondandlevy. The $595,400,000 of general obligation bonds will be repaid from annual excess property taxes sufficient to pay bond debt service over a maximum term of 21 years. Exemptions from taxes may be available to certain homeowners. For more information, contact the King County Department of Assessments, 206-296-3920.

provenance.quote:
Highline School District No. 401
Proposition No. 1 Bonds to Replace and Rebuild Deteriorating Schools and Improve Safety
The Board of Directors of Highline School District No. 401 adopted Resolution No. 11-26, concerning neighborhood school improvements and safety upgrades. This proposition would authorize the District to: replace or rebuild four deteriorating schools (Cascade, Chinook, Sylvester, CHOICE Academy), including new career/technical learning spaces, secure entrances, security camera upgrades; make critical districtwide core building system upgrades, including heating, roofing, electrical, plumbing; implement districtwide health, security, fire system and earthquake safety upgrades; issue $595,400,000 of general obligation bonds maturing within 21 years; and levy annual excess property taxes to repay the bonds, all as provided in Resolution No. 11-26. Should this proposition be:
Approved Rejected

measures.questionText:
The Board of Directors of Highline School District No. 401 adopted Resolution No. 12-26, concerning educational technology and capital improvements to maintain student learning. This proposition would fund districtwide technology, programs and staff and other capital improvements not funded by the State, including cybersecurity protections, reliable internet, technology operations and infrastructure, and student/staff technology access, and authorize the District to levy the following excess taxes on all taxable property within the District: Collection Year Estimated Levy Rate/$1,000 Assessed Value Levy Amount 2027 $0.36 $12,000,000 2028 $0.35 $12,000,000 2029 $0.34 $12,000,000 2030 $0.32 $12,000,000 all as provided in Resolution No. 12-26. Should this proposition be approved?
Yes No
measures.officialStatement: Proposition 2 authorizes a capital levy for educational technology and capital improvements to maintain student learning and improve student and staff safety and security. Proposition 2 will address the existing condition of educational technology equipment, infrastructure and systems and aging and educationally outdated school facilities. The capital levy will fund: (1) cybersecurity protections and systems that protect student and staff data; (2) reliable internet, wireless networks and technology infrastructure that support teaching and learning; (3) student and staff devices, classroom technology and instructional software; (4) educator and staff training and support to implement technology improvements; and (5) other technology improvements and upgrades districtwide. The capital levy will also fund districtwide capital improvements to support the construction, modernization and remodeling of schools and facilities. More information is available at highlineschools.org/bondandlevy. The proposed four-year levy would authorize collection of $12,000,000 in each of the years 2027 through 2030. The levy rate per $1,000 of assessed value required to produce these amounts is estimated to be $0.36 in 2027, $0.35 in 2028, $0.34 in 2029, and $0.32 in 2030. Exact levy rates will be determined based on actual assessed value at the time of levy. Exemptions from taxes may be available to certain homeowners. For more information, contact the King County Department of Assessments, 206-296-3920.

measures.questionText:
The Board of Directors of Kent School District No. 415 adopted Resolution No. 1718 concerning a proposition to support educational programs and operations expenses. If approved, this proposition would authorize the District to levy the following excess taxes, replacing an expiring levy, on all taxable property within the District, to support educational programs and operations not funded by the State’s statutory program of basic education. Collection Year Approximate Levy Rate/$1,000 Assessed Value Levy Amount 2028 $1.95 $104,700,000 2029 $1.93 $111,100,000 2030 $1.88 $115,700,000 2031 $1.84 $121,400,000 Should this proposition be approved?
Yes No
measures.officialStatement: Passage of Proposition 1 would allow Kent School District to replace an expiring voter-approved levy for school programs and operations by levying $104,700,000 for collection in 2028, $111,100,000 for collection in 2029, $115,700,000 for collection in 2030, and $121,400,000 for collection in 2031. The proposed levy would replace an existing levy that voters previously approved and expires in 2027. The expiring levy currently funds approximately 15% of the District’s general operating expenses. If approved, the proposed replacement levy would pay for day-to-day school operations to meet student needs not funded by the State, including but not limited to college and career readiness staff and programs, physical, social, and emotional learning staff and programs (including mental health counselors and staff), materials, supplies, and operational costs (including utilities and insurance), transportation, safety and security staff, athletic and extra-curricular programs, electives, and classroom support programs. Based on projected assessed valuation information, the District estimates a tax rate of $1.95 per $1,000 of assessed valuation for 2028; $1.93 per $1,000 of assessed valuation for 2029; $1.88 per $1,000 of assessed valuation for 2030; and $1.84 per $1,000 of assessed valuation for 2031. A property tax exemption may be available to senior or disabled homeowners who meet specified income limits. For information regarding exemptions, call the King County Assessor at (206) 296-3920.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would make Bothell part of the Shoreline Fire Department Regional Fire Authority on March 1, 2027, under the amended regional fire plan in Resolution 1784. Bothell’s fire department would join the regional authority, while current fire and emergency medical service levels would continue. Bothell would have representation on the authority’s board, and its voters would vote on the authority’s future ballot measures, including taxes and benefit charges.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would approve Bothell’s annexation into the regional fire authority under this plan.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject this annexation proposal.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would increase Clyde Hill’s regular property tax levy rate from about $0.30 to no more than $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027 to fund police, fire, emergency medical, 911 dispatch, land-use and zoning services. The total levy amount could then rise by a 3% annual limit factor in 2028–2036, and the 2036 levy would become the base for later years. Qualifying seniors, veterans and people with disabilities would be exempt from the increase. The city estimates the 2027 increase at about $225 for a property assessed at $1 million.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would approve the higher 2027 levy, the 3% annual increase limit for 2028–2036, and use of the 2036 levy as the later tax base.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject these proposed levy changes.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would authorize Issaquah to borrow up to $18 million through general obligation bonds, repaid within 20 years through annual additional property taxes. The money would fund sports fields and courts, new trails and trailhead improvements, restoration of Confluence Park’s Ek House, playground improvements, a new dog park and related park and recreation projects. The city plans to issue these as earlier park bonds retire and estimates an average cost of about $80 a year for a $1 million home. Existing qualifying exemptions for low-income seniors, certain veterans and others would continue.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would authorize the park and recreation bonds and property taxes to repay them.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject this bond and repayment-tax authorization.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would increase Kenmore’s maximum regular property tax rate to $1.25 per $1,000 of assessed value for collection in 2027, funding climate and environmental programs, affordable housing and human services. It would allow the levy amount to rise by up to 6% annually in 2028–2032, subject to the state-law maximum rate, and use the 2032 levy as the base for future levies. Qualifying seniors, veterans and others would be exempt from the increase. The city estimates an added cost of about $30 a month for a home assessed at $1 million.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would approve this property tax increase, the subsequent annual levy increases and the new levy base.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject these proposed levy changes.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would temporarily increase Lake Forest Park’s regular property tax levy for public safety, including police, safety equipment, 911 dispatch, emergency management, jail services and mental health crisis response. The maximum total regular levy rate would be $0.88920 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027. The increase could rise with Seattle-area consumer-price inflation for the next five years, 2028–2032, after a public process and council vote. When it expires, the levy would return to what it would have been without this increase. Qualifying low-income seniors, disabled veterans and other people with disabilities would be exempt. The city estimates the increase at $0.22 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would approve this temporary public-safety property tax increase and its inflation adjustments.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject this levy increase.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would raise Milton’s sales and use tax by 0.1 percentage point beginning in 2027, adding 10 cents to a taxable $100 purchase. Revenue would provide ongoing funding for police and other public-safety purposes allowed by state law, including law-enforcement staffing. The city would have to share 15% of these tax proceeds with the county.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would approve this sales and use tax increase for public safety.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject the proposed tax increase.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would raise SeaTac’s sales and use tax by 0.1 percentage point to fund fire protection and prevention, emergency medical response, law-enforcement staffing, criminal justice, public-safety operations and other city services allowed by law. This would add 10 cents to a taxable $100 purchase. The city would receive 85% of the revenue and King County 15%; at least one-third would have to fund fire protection, criminal justice, or both. Most groceries, motor-vehicle sales and the first 36 months of vehicle leases would be exempt from this tax.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would authorize this sales and use tax increase with the stated revenue-sharing and spending requirements.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject the proposed tax increase.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would create a Shoreline Metropolitan Park District with the same boundaries as the city and a governing board made up of city councilmembers. It would fund a new indoor pool facility and possible future recreational facilities, including construction, operation, maintenance, renovation and expansion. Revenue could be used only for those facilities, rather than other city needs. The district could levy property taxes up to $0.75 per $1,000 of assessed value; the anticipated starting rate is $0.55, or the amount needed to raise about $8.8 million a year. Collection would begin in 2028.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A FOR vote would create the park district with these taxing and recreation-facility powers.
measureRecords.noMeans: An AGAINST vote would reject creation of this park district.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would authorize Auburn School District to borrow up to $491 million through general obligation bonds, repaid within 20 years through annual additional property taxes. The money would build and equip a new middle school and larger replacement schools for Cascade Middle School and Alpac Elementary, with safety, technology, energy-efficiency and playfield improvements. The district expects about $36,248,500 in state construction assistance if voters approve. A property tax exemption may be available to qualifying senior or disabled homeowners.
measureRecords.yesMeans: An APPROVED vote would authorize the school-construction bonds and property taxes to repay them.
measureRecords.noMeans: A REJECTED vote would reject this bond and repayment-tax authorization.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would authorize Highline School District to borrow $595.4 million through general obligation bonds, repaid within 21 years through annual additional property taxes. It would replace Cascade and Sylvester middle schools, partly rebuild and modernize Chinook Middle School, and rebuild the former Southern Heights Elementary site for CHOICE Academy. It would also fund building-system, security, fire-system, earthquake-safety and accessibility work across the district, plus design plans for Valley View Early Learning Center and Hilltop Elementary. Qualifying homeowners may be eligible for property tax exemptions.
measureRecords.yesMeans: An APPROVED vote would authorize these school-construction and safety bonds and property taxes to repay them.
measureRecords.noMeans: A REJECTED vote would reject this bond and repayment-tax authorization.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would authorize Highline School District to collect an additional $12 million in property taxes each year from 2027 through 2030 for educational technology, programs and staff, and capital improvements not funded by the state. Work includes cybersecurity, internet and technology infrastructure, student and staff devices, instructional software, training, and school-facility improvements. Estimated rates per $1,000 of assessed value are $0.36 in 2027, $0.35 in 2028, $0.34 in 2029 and $0.32 in 2030; actual rates would depend on assessed values. Qualifying homeowners may be eligible for exemptions.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would authorize this four-year technology and capital-improvements levy.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject this levy authorization.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would replace Kent School District’s levy that expires in 2027 with property taxes for educational programs and operating costs not paid for by the state’s basic-education program. Collections would be $104.7 million in 2028, $111.1 million in 2029, $115.7 million in 2030 and $121.4 million in 2031. Estimated rates per $1,000 of assessed value are $1.95, $1.93, $1.88 and $1.84 respectively. The money would support day-to-day operations, including counselors, learning and career programs, transportation, safety, athletics, extracurricular activities and classroom support. Qualifying senior or disabled homeowners may be eligible for an exemption.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would authorize this replacement school-programs and operations levy for 2028–2031.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject this replacement levy.
